## Data Generating Process

The simulations are a fully factored experiment. 

**Block Level Fixed Covariates**  
Number of Blocks: 5;  ATE: .2; ICC: .2; Average Number of Observations Per Cluster: 20; Proportion of Clusters Treated: .5 (this is fixed across blocks); Number of District Level Covariates: 0


**Block Level Varying Covariates (Factors that are varied across simulations)**

Three groups of block level parameters Blocks all the same, Blocks all messy, and Blocks all reasonable

Blocks all the same: How much do number clusters per block vary (size ratio)?: 0 (none); How much does the size of the cluster vary (size ratio)? 0 (none); ATE SD: 0; Correlation Between Treatment Effect and Cluster Size: 0; Correlation Between Average Number of Observations Per Cluster and Total Number of Clusters: 0; Correlation of Proportion of Clusters Treated per Block and Impact: 0; Correlation Between Outcome Intercept and Cluster Size: 0

Blocks all messy: How much do number clusters per block vary (size ratio)?: 1.3 (big) ; How much does the size of the cluster vary (size ratio)? 1.3 (big); ATE SD: .6; Correlation Between Treatment Effect and Cluster Size: .8; Correlation Between Average Number of Observations Per Cluster and Total Number of Clusters: .8; Correlation of Proportion of Clusters Treated per Block and Impact: .8; Correlation Between Outcome Intercept and Cluster Size: .8

Blocks all reasonable: How much do number clusters per block vary (size ratio)?: .4 (average); How much does the size of the cluster vary (size ratio)? .4 (average); ATE SD: .1; Correlation Between Treatment Effect and Cluster Size: .2; Correlation Between Average Number of Observations Per Cluster and Total Number of Clusters: .1; Correlation of Proportion of Clusters Treated per Block and Impact: 0; Correlation Between Outcome Intercept and Cluster Size: .1

Each of the rest of these factors don't vary as a group but vary each individually and are fully factored with all other factors:

Average Number of Clusters per Block: 4,8,16

**Cluster Level Varying Parameters**

Correlation of Impact and Size of Cluster: 0, .8

Cluster Level Treatment Effect Standard Deviation: 0, .3

Cluster Level ICC: 0, .2

Number of Observations Per Cluster Varies: True, False 

Ratio of Size Cluster Sizes: 0, .4, 1.3 

Number of School-Level Covariates: 0, 1, 5

[School Level Covariate R Squared is always .5]

```{r dataprep, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
# Function to create labeled factors with zero as base level
create_labeled_factor <- function(x) {
  unique_values <- sort(unique(x))
  num_levels <- length(unique_values)
  
  if (num_levels == 1) {
    # If only one level, just return as is
    return(factor(x))
  } else if (num_levels == 2) {
    # For two levels: 0 (base) and "L" (for larger value)
    labels <- c("0", "L")
    return(factor(x, levels = unique_values, labels = labels))
  } else if (num_levels == 3) {
    # For three levels: 0 (base), "S" (small/middle), and "L" (large)
    labels <- c("0", "S", "L")
    return(factor(x, levels = unique_values, labels = labels))
  } else {
    # For more than three levels, label by position
    # Zero is always the base (first level), and others are numbered
    zero_pos <- which(unique_values == 0)
    if (length(zero_pos) > 0) {
      # Reorder so 0 is first
      ordered_levels <- c(0, unique_values[unique_values != 0])
      labels <- c("0", paste0("L", 1:(num_levels-1)))
      return(factor(x, levels = ordered_levels, labels = labels))
    } else {
      # If no zero value exists, just use ordered values
      warning("No zero value found in variable. Using smallest value as base.")
      labels <- c("0", paste0("L", 1:(num_levels-1)))
      return(factor(x, levels = unique_values, labels = labels))
    }
  }
}

#figure out which estimators produce the same ATE results 

group_estimators <- function( rps,var ) {
  
  wid <-rps %>% dplyr::select( ID, method, all_of(var) ) %>% 
    pivot_wider( names_from = method, values_from = var ) %>%
    dplyr::select( -ID)
  
  results <- combn(names(wid), 2, function(x) {
    mean_diff <- mean(wid[[x[1]]] - wid[[x[2]]])
    tibble(pair = paste(x, collapse = " - "), mean_difference = round( mean_diff, digits=10 ) )
  }, simplify = FALSE) %>% bind_rows()
  
  
  # Create a matrix where each element is the mean difference between two columns
  mean_diff_matrix <- outer(1:ncol(wid), 1:ncol(wid), Vectorize(function(x, y) {
    abs( mean(wid[[x]] - wid[[y]]) )
  }))
  
  # Naming rows and columns for clarity
  colnames(mean_diff_matrix) <- names(wid)
  rownames(mean_diff_matrix) <- names(wid)
  
  mean_diff_matrix
  
  # Assuming mean_diff_matrix is your matrix of pairwise mean differences
  tolerance <- 10^-7
  
  # Create a binary matrix where 1 indicates differences below the tolerance
  binary_matrix <- 0 + (mean_diff_matrix < tolerance)
  binary_matrix
  
  # Convert this binary matrix into a list of groups
  groups <- list()
  already_included <- c()
  
  ests = sort( rownames(binary_matrix) )
  for (i in ests) {
    if (!( i %in% already_included)) {
      # Find indices where the estimator is within tolerance of others
      in_group <- which(binary_matrix[i, ] == 1)
      group_names <- colnames(binary_matrix)[in_group]
      groups[[length(groups) + 1]] <- group_names
      already_included <- c(already_included, group_names)
    }
  }
  groups
}
```

## What does the bias look like for each estimator 

The estimators that theory says should be biased are in fact much more biased across the simulations. These boxplots are across the different data generating processes, each dot is the mean bias across simulation replications. The methods in light blue are the ones theory says should be biased. I only show the finite population numbers because they are the same as the super population results. 

There are tables showing how the different simulation facets predict bias. The regression model is how each facet of the data generating process predicts mean bias against a methods targeted estimand. The facets are binary indicators and are fully interacted with each other. I ran three models: just the cluster targeted methods, just the person targeted methods, and all methods. I don't know what to make of the results.

```{r biasmodel, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
# Helper function to add significance stars
  add_stars <- function(p_value) {
    if (is.na(p_value)) return("")
    if (p_value < 0.001) return("***")
    if (p_value < 0.01) return("**") 
    if (p_value < 0.05) return("*")
    if (p_value < 0.1) return(".")
    return("")
  }
  
# Create comparison table with significance stars
create_star_comparison_table <- function(model_list) {

  # Initialize a list to store tidy model outputs
  tidy_models <- list()
  
  # Process each model
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    # Get model coefficients and p-values
    model_stats <- tidy(model_list[[m]]) %>%
      # Create a column with coefficient and stars without parentheses
      mutate(
        stars = sapply(p.value, add_stars),
        coef_stars = sprintf("%.3f%s", estimate, stars)
      )
    
    # Add to our list
    tidy_models[[m]] <- model_stats
  }
  
  # Combine all models into a single data frame
  all_terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(tidy_models, function(x) x$term)))
  
  # Initialize result dataframe
  result <- data.frame(term = all_terms)
  
  # Add each method's coefficients as a column
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    temp_df <- tidy_models[[m]] %>% 
      select(term, coef_stars)
    
    # Rename to method name
    names(temp_df)[2] <- m
    
    # Join to result
    result <- result %>% 
      left_join(temp_df, by = "term")
  }
  
  return(result)
}


# Add a footnote explaining significance levels
add_significance_footnote <- function(table_object) {
  footnote(table_object,
    general = "Significance codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1",
    general_title = "Note: "
  )
}

# Function to create comparison table
create_comparison_table <- function(model_list) {
  # Initialize a list to store tidy model outputs
  tidy_models <- list()
  
  # Process each model
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    # Get model coefficients and p-values
    model_stats <- tidy(model_list[[m]]) %>%
      # Create a column with coefficient and p-value together
      mutate(coef_pval = sprintf("%.3f (p=%.3f)", estimate, p.value))
    
    # Add to our list
    tidy_models[[m]] <- model_stats
  }
  
  # Combine all models into a single data frame
  all_terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(tidy_models, function(x) x$term)))
  
  # Initialize result dataframe
  result <- data.frame(term = all_terms)
  
  # Add each method's coefficients as a column
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    temp_df <- tidy_models[[m]] %>% 
      select(term, coef_pval)
    
    # Rename to method name
    names(temp_df)[2] <- m
    
    # Join to result
    result <- result %>% 
      left_join(temp_df, by = "term")
  }
  
  return(result)
}

# Create simplified version with main effects only
create_main_effects_table <- function(model_list) {
  # Initialize a list to store tidy model outputs
  tidy_models <- list()
  
  # Process each model
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    # Get model coefficients and p-values
    model_stats <- tidy(model_list[[m]]) %>%
      # Filter for main effects only (terms without ":")
      filter(!grepl(":", term)) %>%
      # Create a column with coefficient and p-value together
      mutate(coef_pval = sprintf("%.3f (p=%.3f)", estimate, p.value))
    
    # Add to our list
    tidy_models[[m]] <- model_stats
  }
  
  # Combine all models into a single data frame
  all_terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(tidy_models, function(x) x$term)))
  
  # Initialize result dataframe
  result <- data.frame(term = all_terms)
  
  # Add each method's coefficients as a column
  for (m in names(model_list)) {
    temp_df <- tidy_models[[m]] %>% 
      select(term, coef_pval)
    
    # Rename to method name
    names(temp_df)[2] <- m
    
    # Join to result
    result <- result %>% 
      left_join(temp_df, by = "term")
  }
  
  return(result)
}
```

## What does the RMSE look like for each estimator 

As far as I can tell the RMSE actually looks pretty similar across estimators, which is consistent with the idea of there being a bias variance trade off. Unlike with the bias, the finite population RMSEs are fairly different from the super population RMSEs. 

Like above, the boxplots are across the different data generating processes, each dot is a mean across simulation replications. The methods in light blue are those classified to be biased by theory. The ratio of finite RMSE to super RMSE plots show the ratio of RMSE from the finite population models over the super population models, and are designed to show that these are different.

## What does the coverage look like for each estimator 

Coverage is the percentage of simulation replications where the estimator is within the 95% confidence interval. We would like the number to 95% (the boxplots have a red line at there). The notable things are that the coverage for the MLM estimators is often very bad but other than that the coverage for the cluster weighted estimators is generally good. The coverage rates for the person weighted estimators however are pretty bad across methods,it's either very low (meaning the SEs are being underestimated) or too high (meaning the SEs are being overestimated within the same methods. In addition, finite versus super makes very little difference for the cluster targeted estimators but makes a noticeable difference for the person weighted estimators. 



```{r cov, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE}

ggplot(sruns.full_factor %>% filter(weight=="Cluster"), aes(x = method, y = cover.f.sch*100, color = biased)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 95, color="red", linewidth=.75)+
  labs(
    title = "Coverage by Method, Cluster Weighted Finite Population",
    x = "Method",
    y = "Coverage, Cluster Weighted Finite Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8)) +
    coord_flip()
```

## What do the standard errors look like for each estimator

Standard error inflation is the ration of the estimated standard error over the true standard error. High inflation means the standard errors are too big and low inflation means the standard errors are too small. 

For some of the methods the standard error estimates are way off, but it does not seem obviously driven by low degrees of freedom. The true finite standard errors do not look to be the same as the true super standard errors. 

```{r infl, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE}

ggplot(sruns.full_factor, aes(x = method, y = log(inflate.f), color = weight)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Standard Error Inflation by Method, Finite Population",
    x = "Method",
    y = "Log of Standard Error Inflation, Finite Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme( axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8)) +
  coord_flip()

ggplot(sruns.full_factor, aes(x = mean.df, y = log(inflate.f), color = method)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Standard Error Inflation versus Mean Degrees of Freedom, Finite Population",
    x = "Mean Degrees of Freedom",
    y = "Log Standard Error Inflation, Finite Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size=12),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 1, r = 1, b = 1, l = 1),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
    legend.box.margin = margin(t = 20),
    legend.spacing.y = unit(0.1, "lines"),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.8, "lines"),
    legend.title = element_blank()
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(x = c(0, 250))

ggplot(sruns.full_factor, aes(x = method, y = log(inflate.s), color = weight)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Standard Error Inflation by Method, Super Population",
    x = "Method",
    y = "Log Standard Error Inflation, Super Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme( axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))+
  coord_flip()


ggplot(sruns.full_factor, aes(x = mean.df, y = log(inflate.s), color = method)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Standard Error Inflation versus Mean Degrees of Freedom, Super Population",
    x = "Mean Degrees of Freedom",
    y = "Log Standard Error Inflation, Super Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0,size=12),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 1, r = 1, b = 1, l = 1),

  ) +
```
